ac3ee12213336cdb: Asus has warned eShop customers that an intruder got into part of its online store and may have helped themselves to contact details and order records. The PC maker disclosed the incident in an email sent to customers, first reported by KitGuru, in which it said had identified "unauthorized access to part of the Asus eShop environment," although exactly when that access occurred remains unclear. "Our investigation indicates that certain customer order information, including contact details and order records, may have been accessed," the company said. There is at least some good news for anyone who has handed Asus their card details. The company said no payment card, bank account, or other financial information was involved in the breach. Asus also said it isn't currently aware of the compromised information being misused or of any affected customers suffering harm. The company said it took steps to contain the incident after discovering the unauthorized access, launched an investigation, and introduced additional measures to secure the affected systems. That investigation remains ongoing, but Asus said it had found no evidence of continued unauthorized access. What Asus hasn't said is how many customers are caught up in the mess, when the intrusion began, how long the attacker had access, which countries are affected, or how whoever was behind the break-in managed to get into the eShop environment in the first place. The details that did escape, however, could give scammers a decent head start. Asus warned that the stolen details could give scammers enough to make phishing emails, texts, and phone calls about its products or customers' orders look rather more convincing. Asus told customers to keep an eye out for unexpected messages mentioning previous purchases, though it reckons the risk of anyone actually misusing the data remains low. This isn't the PC maker's first recent brush with data thieves. In December, Asus confirmed that one of its suppliers had been hacked after the Everest ransomware gang claimed to have pinched 1 TB of data from itself, ArcSoft, and Qualcomm. The company said the haul included some camera source code used in its phones, but maintained that its own systems and customer data were untouched. The Register asked Asus for more details about the latest breach, including how many customers were affected and when and how the intrusion occurred, but has not yet received a response. Asus is yet to comment publicly on the incident, and there is no mention of the breach on its eShop. So it's the usual post-breach drill: beware unexpected emails, texts, and calls. Except this time, whoever's behind them may have the receipts. ®
cea08b8af0c55cda: DESPERATE FOR SHELTER

IN her Gaza City apartment, Heba Arafat walks uphill across a living room slanted at a steep angle after Israeli airstrikes caused the building's foundations to collapse, leaving the entire structure tilted.

Like thousands of people in Gaza, Arafat chose to risk living in an apartment building damaged during nearly three years of war between Israel and Hamas, with countless Israeli airstrikes on the Palestinian territory.
"We were forced to live here because we had nowhere else to go. All of our homes were destroyed, our land was razed and we have nothing left," said Arafat, 47.

According to the United Nations, 84 per cent of all structures in Gaza had been damaged or destroyed by last October, and Gaza's civil defence says 2,000 buildings across the territory are at risk of collapse.
Last week, 21 people, including 12 children, died in Gaza City after a six-storey building, which local authorities said had been hit repeatedly by Israeli air-strikes, collapsed.

Arafat lives with her six daughters and husband in their old apartment building in Gaza City's Al-Shati Refugee Camp, which they left at the height of the war that began in October 2023 with Hamas's attack on Israel.

The family returned after a ceasefire last October. They found that their four-storey building, in which 30 people now live, had collapsed inwards at the ground floor, the result, she said, of an Israeli ground operation in the area.
Like most buildings in Gaza City, the windows were blown away by blasts, with makeshift bedsheets spread across the frames providing little privacy.
As she spoke, Arafat illustrated her building's slant by leaving a water bottle sideways on the floor, only for it to quickly roll away to the other end of the room.

While no territory-wide estimate exists, Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN humanitarian coordinator for the Palestinian territories, said last week people across Gaza were living in "hundreds of damaged and unsafe shelters".
"Where can we go? Even though this house is dangerous," Arafat said. "We have been terrified ever since we heard about houses collapsing. The danger has become even greater than we thought".
Gaza City municipal staff patrol the streets to identify buildings at risk of collapse and mark them with stencils.

"These homes pose a genuine threat to the lives of the displaced persons sheltering inside them, as well as to residents in the vicinity and those in nearby displacement camps," said Hosni Muhanna, a Gaza City spokesperson.
But Muhanna knows that people are likely to remain in these buildings for lack of better options.

"Thousands of displaced people are forced to seek shelter in these dilapidated buildings on the verge of collapse to escape the hardships of displacement camps that offer no protection against the summer heat or winter cold."

Most Gaza residents were displaced at least once during the war, and many of them remain in enormous camps for the displaced, in tents provided by humanitarian organisations or in improvised shelters.

With diseases such as the skin infection impetigo rampaging through certain camps due to the lack of waste disposal and general overcrowding, many Gaza residents have found it safer to take the risks of moving into the damaged buildings.
And with Gaza's economy in tatters, many remain dependent on aid, which Israel has allowed into Gaza with restrictions since the declaration of the US-brokered ceasefire last October.

But Israel has kept carrying out airstrikes, and has restricted the entry of a range of equipment that it says could also have military use, but which Gazans and international NGOs say are needed for the territory's vast reconstruction needs.

These can include large machinery needed to clear rubble from the site of destroyed buildings, or spare parts and lubricants needed to keep other tools running, UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said in August.
With the ceasefire process stalled for months, reconstruction efforts planned under the ceasefire have yet to begin.
According to a joint assessment published by the UN, World Bank and European Union in April, Gaza will require US$71.4 billion in recovery and reconstruction spending over the next decade.
"We're afraid a wall or the roof might fall on us, so we huddle together, afraid one of us might get hurt," Arafat said.

eeede90db44fa7fa: KANGAR: The Perlis Immigration Department detained 10 Thai nationals suspected of being involved in online gambling activities during Op Sapu at a house in Taman Choo Kee today.
Perlis Immigration director Mohammad A'sim Md Ali said those detained comprised six men and four women aged between 23 and 36.

He said the operation, conducted at about 12.40am, was the result of a month-long intelligence gathering and surveillance by the department's Intelligence and Special Operations Division following suspicious activities believed to involve foreigners at the premises.
"After the target was identified and information obtained, a team of enforcement officers was deployed to the location to conduct inspections and enforcement action.

"Upon arrival, the team found the door locked and received no response from the occupants despite knocking several times. The team then gained access to the premises to conduct the inspection," he said in a statement tonight.
A'sim said upon entering the premises, several occupants attempted to flee and hide in various parts of the house to evade inspection, but all were located and detained.
He said based on initial inspections and the discovery of equipment at the scene, the 10 Thai nationals found on the premises were suspected of being involved in online gambling activities.

"Checks through the department's system revealed that all they possessed valid Social Visit Passes. However, they are suspected of carrying out activities contrary to the pass conditions and were detained to assist in investigations under Regulation 39(b) of the Immigration Regulations 1963," he said.
During the operation, he added, the team also seized 22 mobile phones, seven laptops, and 10 Thai passports for further investigation.
A'sim said that possessing a valid pass or travel document does not grant foreigners permission to work or engage in activities that violate the conditions of the pass.

He stressed that the Perlis Immigration Department would continue to step up enforcement operations based on intelligence, surveillance, and public information to ensure compliance with immigration laws and regulations.
99bea8bc4d68d188: SEPANG: Former Formula One driver Alex Yoong has known enough setbacks in motor racing to savour the moment his protege, Taj Izrin Aiman Taj Madira, became an Asian Games champion.

"I had tears in my eyes during the race when we could see Taj was going to win gold," Alex said on his arrival at Kuala Lumpur International Airport today.
"We had worked very hard, and I was so happy to see it pay off."
Alex said the result showed what a focused preparation programme could do for Malaysian sim racing.

He thanked the Youth and Sports Ministry and the Malaysia Esports Federation (MESF) for helping the drivers train for the Asian Games, including at the National Sports Institute in Bukit Jalil and with the National Sports Council.
"That made a huge difference. For the first time, the sim racing community had a targeted programme, and the drivers could concentrate on preparing for this event," he said.

Alex said there had been doubts earlier this year that Malaysia could challenge drivers from Japan, Saudi Arabia and South Korea, but Taj Izrin's progress became clear in the final two weeks before the Games.
"People said at the start of the year that winning gold was impossible. We knew it could be done," he said.
The victory also brought back memories of Alex's own losses.
He said those experiences had shaped the way he coached young drivers to keep working and enjoy the process, whatever the result.
Taj Izrin will receive a RM20,000 reward from the MESF for winning a gold at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
2d0c74b7a0b703d3: EVENT: HPE and NVIDIA are sending their AI infrastructure leads to a dinner table in Washington where nothing said is on the record. The Register is hosting, our editor-in-chief Matt Rosoff takes the chair, and there is one table, on Thursday 29 October. Most AI programs in regulated industries do not stall on the model. They stall on where the data lives, who can reach it, and what an auditor will accept as evidence a year from now. Sovereignty is not one requirement either: what can leave a jurisdiction and what can leave the building are different questions with different owners. The proprietary data that makes an AI system worth building is the same data that makes it a risk to build, and the boundary drawn around a pilot quietly becomes the boundary around production. Those calls get made on what people will tell you in private. What a bank had to rebuild. What a hospital group's legal team refused to sign. Which sovereign option somebody paid for and would not buy again. None of that gets said on a recorded webinar, or in a briefing with a deck. So this is neither. Chatham House Rule, three questions, dinner, no slides. Everyone at the table is there as a peer, the vendors included, and the chair's job includes redirecting anyone who starts to pitch. On the table: which infrastructure options actually hold a boundary, what each one costs in capital, in capability or in elasticity, and whether any of it survives the move from first planning to running operations. HPE sends Thierry Pienaar, HPE Fellow and Chief Technology Officer for HPC and AI Worldwide Sales. NVIDIA sends Bert Condensa, Vice President for Enterprise AI Factory Segment Sales. They are there to answer, not to present. The table is for technology, data and risk leaders in healthcare, financial services, research, pharmaceuticals, government and higher education who are making these decisions now rather than next year. Dinner runs from 6.00pm to 8.30pm at Fiola Mare. Places are limited and go by invitation. Request one here. Government and public sector guests: where your agency's ethics rules require it, you can pay your own share and we will provide a receipt. Please say so when you request an invitation.

5ac20f7e9de286f9: NAGOYA: Japanese wunderkind Shin Ohashi followed in the slipstream of China's Yu Zidi to become the latest teenage sensation to set the Asian Games pool alight on Thursday, shattering the men's 200 metres breaststroke world record.

A day after 13-year-old Yu capped her fairytale Asian Games debut with a hat-trick of golds, 17-year-old Ohashi produced a blistering 2:04.83 to eclipse the mark of 2:05.48 set by China's Qin Haiyang at the 2023 world championships in Fukuoka.
It came little more than a week after Ohashi fell ill with COVID-19, which he said may have been a blessing in disguise.
"The world record was my goal so I'm very happy to get it," hesaid at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre.
"My next goal is for the gold medal at the world championships," added the teenager, showing why French superstar Leon Marchand views the Japanese prodigy as a serious rival.
"I'm scared. I'm very scared of him," Olympic 200m breaststroke champion Marchand said of Ohashi earlier this week.
"He's still so young. His coach is really good. I think his entourage, the people around him, are really good, so I hope he's going to keep improving."
Zhang Zhanshuo won his sixth gold of the Aichi-Nagoya Games after helping China to the men's 4x100m freestyle relay title.

Elsewhere, Carlos Yulo, the Philippines' first Olympic gymnastics champion, added an Asian Games title to his trophy cabinet with victory in the floor exercise, and felt redemption after disappointment at Jakarta 2018.

Yulo, who honed his craft in Japan on a scholarship from the local Olympic committee, scored 14.666 to edge Kazakhstan's Milad Karimi (14.600) in a cliffhanger. His brother Karl Eldrew also competed in the final.
The 26-year-old was delighted to complete a career grand slam of world, Olympic and continental crowns.
"This medal, it's like winning the Olympics," Yulo told Reuters. "It's really a good story, and I feel like I redeemed it in this competition."
Eight-times Olympian Oksana Chusovitina missed out on a medal at the age of 51, coming fifth in the women's vault final, 32 years after she took bronze at Hiroshima 1994.
But the Uzbek said Nagoya would spur her on to try to qualify for a ninth Olympics at Los Angeles 2028.
"Honestly, I get so much enjoyment out of seeing the crowd and stepping onto the podium. It brings me immense pleasure, and that's why I keep going."
CHINA'S GOLD RUSH
Sporting powerhouse China continued their imperious march through the multi-sport event, breaching the 75-gold mark.

On the shooting range, Jiang Yiting held her nerve with her final shot to complete a hat-trick of golds at the Aichi-Nagoya Games. The 22-year-old's poise denied South Korea and earned China the skeet mixed team title, adding to her individual and women's team victories.
China also commanded the trails, with Wu Zhifan and Liang Zhenglan securing a one-two finish in the women's cross-country mountain bike final.

Away from the competition venues, local organisers spent another day defending the athletes' accommodation after local residents added their voices to concerns over the shipping container-style modular units.

Organisers scrapped the original plans for a dedicated Athletes' Village to control costs, housing 17,000 athletes and officials across a mix of hotels, container-style modular units and a cruise ship instead.
Several athletes have voiced dissatisfaction over the cramped dimensions of their cabins and beds - a criticism echoed by local residents who toured a prototype unit near the Nagoya TV Tower.
"Once inside, I noticed that the space was quite long and narrow," 49-year-old nurse Wada, who shared only her surname, told Reuters.
Asian Games Organising Committee official Yuta Matsuo, however, maintained that athlete feedback had been taken into consideration from the very beginning. --REUTERS

4df937387dfe193e: A proposal to make KDE an "AI-native" desktop has gone down like a house on fire: screams, flames, people running for safety. There may be no survivors.* Last weekend was KDE's annual Akademy conference and it included a presentation proposing an AI-native KDE. We noted that it seemed likely to polarize the audience. It looks like this was a considerable understatement. In the days since, a debate over proposed restrictions on LLM-assisted contributions descended into bans and a deleted thread. An outside campaign called for KDE to prohibit AI altogether, a GNOME developer proposed a similar policy for that project, and KDE developer Nate Graham apologized for his role in the uproar. The Akademy talk was titled "A lovable, sovereign, AI-native KDE" and the slide deck [PDF] is now available. It ends by saying: "The question is not whether AI. It is how. You choose how much AI – and which." It seems almost calculated to provoke an argument rather than invite discussion. We do not know if the authors intended this – we attempted to contact both of them, but they have not yet responded. Graham opened a discussion on Invent, KDE's GitLab instance, about proposed restrictions on LLM-assisted contributions. Although we are not a member, we watched this with some interest over the weekend. It rapidly became heated. Moderators issued warnings, restricted further comments, and eventually removed the thread. There is an archive of the discussion, but we warn you, it contains some highly offensive language, albeit censored by the member who quoted another member's tweets on X. As events unfolded, the participant who drew attention to the posts was banned first. The author of the offensive material was banned later after their identity was verified. The discussion is gone, but the argument continues. One response was an outside initiative called KDE for People, which called on the KDE project to adopt a No-AI policy. Around 250 people signed it before its organizers closed it to further signatures. GNOME developer Jordan Petridis has also published The GNOME LLM Policy That I Want, proposing that LLMs be barred from creating or modifying anything submitted to GNOME or hosted on its infrastructure. This mentions the recent ballot on AI usage in Debian. We reported on the developer referendum about a month ago, noting that the broad spread of anti-AI options in the ballot was likely to split the vote. (This likelihood was dismissed in the comments.) Well, as The Register's Asia-Pacific desk reported a few days later, Debian did not ban AI contributions. Graham subsequently explained his involvement in a post titled KDE and AI, and you, and me. He opens by saying: "So I accidentally triggered an online shitstorm in the process of trying to craft a set of more restrictive LLM usage guidelines for KDE. Sorry about that." He notes that the Akademy talk met "what I'm told was a fairly chilly reception" and that "the next day, a workshop was held about the topic, also receiving a chilly reception." Every couple of years, the KDE project sets three goals for the next two years. Earlier this week, after Akademy, it chose its latest three: you can see them in the last column of the goal-setting Kanban board. The ones chosen are: KDE for Enterprise and Deployments (Issue #5) Better documentation (Issue #2) Next Generation Styling for KDE (Issue #3) We see no mention of AI in there. In context, that may come as a relief to parts of the community. Bootnote *A tip of the black Borsalino to the late great Terry Pratchett, for two different "house on fire" references we combined. ®
2c1c1684497f509b: KUALA LUMPUR: Zaki Ubaidillah conquered his nerves to deliver the winning point as Indonesia fought back from the brink to stun China 3-2 and end a 28-year wait for the Asian Games men's badminton team gold on Thursday.
The Games debutant beat Weng Hong Yang 23-21, 21-13 in 51 minutes at the Ichinomiya City Municipal Gymnasium, completing a remarkable recovery sparked by fellow debutant Alwi Farhan.
Indonesia secured their sixth title and first since Bangkok 1998, denying the defending champions a third successive crown.
"There was definitely pressure, and I felt nervous at the beginning," said Zaki.
"However, I kept reassuring myself to stay calm on the court, and the coaches also helped me stay focused and composed."

China had moved within one victory of gold after Shi Yuqi beat Jonatan Christie 21-13, 21-18 in 47 minutes and Liang Wei Keng–Wang Chang overcame Fajar Alfian–Shohibul Fikri 22-20, 19-21, 21-14 in 71 minutes.
With Indonesia needing all three remaining matches, Alwi kept their challenge alive by defeating Li Shi Feng 23-21, 15-21, 21-16 in an 87-minute second singles battle.
Leo Rolly Carnando–Daniel Marthin then beat He Ji Ting–Liu Yi 23-21, 21-10 in 44 minutes to level the tie and hand Zaki the chance to seal gold.
Zaki edged the opening game before winning the second comfortably, completing the comeback against the reigning Thomas Cup champions.
"I talked to myself, reminding myself that I am capable, that I wanted to keep fighting, and that I needed to bring out all the abilities I prepared from the start."
The triumph offered redemption for Indonesia after their first Thomas Cup group-stage elimination in April, following a 4-1 defeat by France.

407b67cc2c3f40cf: It’s a big week for Meta. The company just kicked off its big Connect conference on Wednesday, and the new Muse AI agent appears to be an early hit. I’ve been using it — it is surprisingly good.

CEO Mark Zuckerberg has obviously been out there taking a victory lap and participating in a lot of interviews about all this. So of course, we asked for him to appear on Decoder. Meta declined my interview request for whatever reason. But luckily Mark just did a big interview with our friend and former colleague Alex Heath on the Sources podcast.

So I figure we could just highlight some moments from that conversation and I could point out some obvious gaps in what Mark is saying about the company right now, and hopefully the next set of people who get to talk to him can ask him some follow-up questions.
So here’s some of the things I would love to ask Mark Zuckerberg if he would join me here on Decoder. Let’s start with Mark’s comments on the Meta Glasses.
Mark Zuckerberg: So we actually feel quite good about the product. I mean, phones don’t have a light, but I mean, people go around recording people all the time.

So I think it’s very important to note that the entire tech industry really wants passive surveillance devices to fit into the same category as phones — for you to understand everything from Flock cameras to Ring doorbells to Meta Glasses the same way that you might understand a smartphone.

Now, there are some very obvious differences here that I think are worth really pushing on in these conversations. For example, if you want to record someone with your phone, you have to take it out of your pocket, open the camera app, and literally hold it in their face. This is a physical action that is meaningfully different from having a pair of glasses on your face with a light and just passively recording someone.

That physical action means that you have to announce your intent to do something with your body and other people can react to it. Obviously, you don’t do that with Meta Glasses. You just start recording and people can notice if there’s a light or not, but the big physical announcement that you’re about to begin recording is not present.

So I think one of the reasons the entire tech industry is so eager to fit these passive surveillance devices into the same kind of mental framework as smartphones is so that no one has to question whether there should be a new social etiquette for these devices. Instead, you’re like, “Oh, it’s just a smartphone. I already understand how to use that.” But importantly, that also brushes over the fact that we did have to create a massive new set of social rules and norms around smartphone recording.

We did live through the entire Black Lives Matter movement because smartphone recording allowed people to record the police, and we as a society didn’t quite know what to do with that information and maybe still don’t know what to do with that information. I would just push on this over and over and over again.

Do you want there to be constant recordings of everyone? Do we think that smartphones allowing everyone to record everything all the time is good? Do we think being able to livestream everything all the time was good? If you could reboot that in a new form factor that allowed for easier and more passive recording, what norms would you change?

There’s already examples of this inside of Meta, where they know the Meta glasses are being used to harass retail workers and women, and they have started down-ranking those videos on Instagram to provide less incentive to make them. So I think a version of this question you could ask very directly is if you know some of the content that is being made with these glasses is so bad that you’ve down-ranked it on your own distribution platform, what is so good about these glasses that make it worth having these debates over and over again?
All right, let’s get back to Mark’s comments on Meta glasses.

Mark Zuckerberg: When we launched the glasses a few years back, we communicated pretty clearly about these steps that we put into it. But like you said, there’s now many, many, many millions of people who’ve gotten the glasses more than had them when we just started launching the product. So I think some of that communication that we did at the beginning, a lot of people either maybe-
Alex Heath: Didn’t see.

Mark Zuckerberg: Or they forgot about it or they didn’t see at the beginning or they just weren’t paying attention to it because the glasses weren’t a big thing. Now that I think we’ve achieved a level of mainstream… well, at a minimum, I think we need to go and make sure that we communicate about what we’re doing and that, yes, we think that this is important and, in fact, so important that we designed it into the product from the very first version that we shipped multiple years ago.

All right, let’s stop here. So I would ask some very simple questions here. What is important? Is it the privacy of the user? Is it the privacy of the person who might be being recorded? And what is it that you thought you were communicating clearly at the beginning that got lost?

What I think Mark is trying to say is at the very beginning, they announced that the glasses would have a light, that the light would be on when you’re recording, that they thought it was obvious that there was a camera in the temple. Over time, as more people got the glasses and more people experienced the glasses on other people’s faces, it was not clear what that light was or what it meant. Now, Mark thinks they have to do more communication about specifically the light existing.

My response to all of that is it doesn’t matter what Meta says. This is the essential truth of every piece of mainstream consumer technology. The users define the product. If you sell millions of gadgets to people, they will use them in ways you never expected. It’s those emergent behaviors that often define the next version of the product.

Probably one of the most famous examples of this is Twitter. Twitter didn’t invent the hashtag or the @ reply or any of a million features that we associate with Twitter. Users on Twitter invented those features, and Twitter adopted them because its users had figured out a way to use the service in ways that it had never even contemplated.

This is broadly true of everything. It’s true of computers, it’s true of smartphones, it’s true of social platforms, and it is true of Meta Glasses. The ways people are using them have nothing to do with Meta’s intentions or its communication about recording lights at the beginning or now.

So I think the natural follow-up question we should all be asking is how much control does Meta have over bad actors who are using these glasses to harass people? Because just telling more people that the light indicates recording isn’t going to stop it.

Are they going to do more things like down-ranking videos of people harassing retail workers? Do they think the other platforms will follow their lead? Does Meta think that creating negative incentives for how people use a camera with content moderation will actually solve the problem? Is there anything about the history of content moderation that suggests that that’s true, given Mark’s own history with content moderation?
Next up, Mark talks about teen safety and Meta’s recent multi-billion dollar teen safety settlement.

Mark Zuckerberg: I think it would’ve been possible to have explained along the way how seriously we took those issues, and we just didn’t because we thought, well, people are showing that by using the product so much they still like the products.

Okay, let me stop there. The claim in many of the social media lawsuits is that the product is addictive. The reason people keep comparing social media to Big Tobacco is that smoking is fun and people enjoyed it, and it was killing them.

So the usage rates had nothing to do with the harm that might’ve been occurring. So from the jump here, I would’ve wanted to push on whether simply measuring usage rates actually lets you measure whether or not something is doing good for the world or good for an individual user.
Mark Zuckerberg: Where we’ve gotten with the social media products, which is both people liking it and understanding how seriously we take all of those issues. So that’s what I aspire to.

Alex Heath: Is there a throughline from that to the recent settlement on all the use safety stuff? I know it’s a thing a lot of people are talking about. Is there any connection from what you just said to that? I would just be curious to hear you reflect on that and what you’ve learned from this process.

Mark Zuckerberg: Yeah, no, I think it’s another good example like this. I mean, we’ve taken a lot of those safety issues seriously for a while and we’ve been working on this teen account work with Instagram for a long time.

So it is true that Meta has done some of the leading work on designing features that would keep kids safer on its platforms. They’ve done some of the leading research in the space on what is actually happening to people on their platforms. And yet one of the dynamics that is particularly galling throughout all of this is that Meta gets punished for it.

So they publish their safety numbers, they publish their research, they publish the amount of bad things that are happening, they do transparency reports. Even if you don’t think that that’s enough, a real thing that continually happens to Meta is they get punished for revealing that bad things happen on their platforms. Companies like Apple, which don’t know what bad things are happening on an encrypted service like iCloud, don’t publish those numbers and don’t get punished for it.

What I would’ve asked Mark here is: How do you solve that dynamic specifically? Because in these lawsuits, it’s been revealed in internal emails that Mark himself has questioned the value of doing the research and building the features because Meta gets punished for it.

So there’s a really strong negative feedback loop here where Meta tries hard and gets punished for it because they’re transparent about it, but in fact, you would want a government regulator to solve it. If all the social media companies were required to be transparent about various metrics around teen safety, then Meta would be judged in comparison to its peers, not for the information existing at all. That doesn’t appear in this settlement.

Instead, what we have is a bunch of behavior controls, product restrictions. Meta seems very keen on making sure those product restrictions connect to TikTok and YouTube, but not on whether we should be able to measure the harms themselves.

So that’s the first thing that I think is worth pushing on: Does this whole industry need to be required to be more transparent about the things happening to children on their platforms? Because if you’re going to make rules and regulations, you should probably start from a common set of information.

Mark Zuckerberg: If you basically said, “Limit usage to an hour a day for teens,” everyone, I think, would be okay with that, except you have to unilaterally do it. If not, then you’re saying, “Okay, if people don’t use Instagram for more than an hour a day, but then their usage goes to TikTok, have we really helped anyone and we’ve just hurt ourselves to not help anyone?”

So what Mark is describing here is a prisoner’s dilemma, where if they take action to make teens safer and TikTok doesn’t, the teens will just go use TikTok and no one will be safe. This idea, of course, is going to come up again when we talk about AI safety, but let’s just talk about social platforms for one minute.

If you believe that there’s a market for safety, if your initial premise was people are using the platform so they must be happy with it, well, then you should make the platform safer for kids, and parents might say to their children, “You’re allowed to use Instagram and not TikTok because Instagram has these controls.” It is very telling to me that Mark doesn’t think there’s a market for safety, that instead he thinks that everyone must be forced to unilaterally disarm by the government in a regulatory framework that solves his prisoner’s dilemma.

So my big question here is: Why is this a problem for the government to solve in social media in a way that might implicate the First Amendment and the speech rights of teenagers, but not a problem for the government to solve in AI safety, where the frontier labs keep talking about killing everyone?

By the way, when I say this connects directly to AI safety, what I mean is that Mark is arguing the opposite side of the prisoner’s dilemma when it comes to AI safety. After all the calls for slowdowns from the various frontier labs, Mark posted a thread on X saying he thought the market would take care of it.

I’ll just read it to you. “My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn’t focus on alignment will fall behind. Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well. Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us. I’m proud of the security foundations we’ve built.”

So straightforwardly, I think the question is why is the go-it-alone approach appropriate when it comes to AI safety, but getting the government to pull the other social media companies into a framework for teen safety appropriate in that market?

The other question I’m just going to steal from my friend Casey Newton, who pointed out that in the most recent teen safety case, Meta estimated its own liability at a trillion dollars in damages, which does not appear to be enough liability for Meta to take unilateral action to prevent teens from being harmed on its platforms. If a trillion dollars in potential liability isn’t enough, how much is enough for Meta to take AI safety seriously? And is there any number in a liability scheme that would stop everyone all at once?
Mark then got into how he plans to run Muse as a business.

Mark Zuckerberg: It, I think, is just going to be able to make people money and save people money… the reason for why we’re doing this is we basically are confident in standing behind the fact that we think that this is going to effectively, for people who are going to use it for running a small business or making money or transactions or commerce in some way, we actually just think it’s going to make so much money for people that the business model over time that we expect is to effectively just take a very small cut of whatever the transaction is.
Alex Heath: A small take-rate business?
Mark Zuckerberg: Yeah, and not even necessarily the person paying for it. It’ll come from the businesses that they’re working with.

So if you’re a Ben Thompson fan or you’ve just listened to enough Decoder, you know that what Zuck is describing here is aggregation theory. He’s going to have all the consumer demand, and it’ll be so big and so lucrative that businesses who want customers will pay Meta a small fee to be on the other side of transactions that happen in Muse.

Being one of the big aggregators is a very lucrative thing. All the big tech giants aggregate demand in one way or another. The problem is the businesses on the other side of the aggregators hate them. Mark knows this better than most because he’s on the other side of one of the biggest aggregators of all — Apple’s App Store. If you want to reach customers on iPhones, you have to go through the Apple App Store and, importantly, agree to a bunch of privacy rules and pay 30 percent fees on most of the transactions that happen on an iPhone.

This hits Meta in two ways. The first is that Apple nearly killed Meta’s ad business with something called App Tracking Transparency when they issued a rule change that really favored Apple’s ad businesses over Meta’s. And two, if you want to boost a post on Instagram from your phone, well, you basically have to pay Apple 30 percent, a fee that Meta breaks out.

Mark hates this so much that he has explicitly talked about building new platforms to get away from Apple for years now. One of the reasons he chased the Metaverse was to build the platform that came after the iPhone and escape Apple. One of the reasons he’s chasing Meta glasses is to build the platform that comes after the iPhone and get away from Apple. And I am dead certain one of the reasons he’s invested so heavily into AI and now Muse is to build the platform that comes after the iPhone and get away from Apple

So the question I would ask Mark here is very simple: How will you make it so all of the businesses downstream of your huge aggregator AI agent feel good about this arrangement? Because when you’ve been in this arrangement, you have felt very, very bad.
Mark also spent some time talking about Meta’s data center investments.

Mark Zuckerberg: So if you look at the data centers, what we’ve actually found is that when a company like Meta goes into a community and makes a commitment that we’re going to invest there for decades, which is really what we’re doing when we’re building up a data center, we’re able to make it so that it’s very good for the community.
I mean, the tax revenue that they bring from that. I mean, in Louisiana, we have this example where the tax revenue funded these $50,000 bonuses for teachers in the community.

Wait, hold on. All right, so this data center in Louisiana, Hyperion… Meta is obviously very proud of it. Mark is talking about the positive impacts it might have for that community. But the actual process of landing that data center deal was basically a bunch of secrecy and backroom deals and huge asks for property tax exemptions from the state government that residents really didn’t know about.

There’s a huge New York Times piece about this project that really goes into detail about the kinds of backroom negotiations that Meta secured in order to go fast and build this data center. So I would simply ask if companies like Meta should lay out these supposed benefits in a much more public and transparent way and let people actually decide for themselves.

Mark Zuckerberg: Of course, you have to design it in a way that can be helpful to people in all these ways, which is also part of the reason why, for people who are skeptical or have so much doom about the whole thing, I mean, one of the things that I basically think is that if we don’t end up building it in a way that’s positive, it just effectively won’t be able to happen.

This is another market argument from Zuck. He’s saying if people don’t like the AI that’s being built or find it helpful, it simply won’t be allowed to exist. The market will kill the products. You can feel a lot of different ways about that, especially if you’ve experienced AI being force-fed to you in your apps and services right now, but I would connect that to social media, where a lot of people felt that social media was doing harm and the industry raced ahead anyway until the government required some regulations.

So I’m once again very curious about Mark’s different postures to government regulation market forces when it comes to social media, where he thinks there should be government regulation, and AI, where he thinks the market should be able to run however it wants.

Secondly, and I think most importantly, I’ve spent a lot of time on this show asking various AI executives if consumer AI products are good enough to overcome doomerism and skepticism. Because right now, they’re not. Even the way Mark describes Muse as being helpful for people running businesses or helping people save money or doing shopping, there’s fundamentally enterprise applications. They’re not big consumer applications that make people overcome their skepticism.

5b8a3fb1942ca873: KUALA LUMPUR: Shareholders of Ajinomoto (Malaysia) Bhd have approved a proposal by its Japanese parent Ajinomoto Co Inc to take the company private through a selective capital reduction and repayment (SCR) exercise at RM20 per share.
The resolution was passed at an extraordinary general meeting today, with 7.85 million shares or 92.84 per cent of the voted shares supporting it, according to a Bursa Malaysia filing.
A total of 216 shareholders voted in favour, while 56 shareholders holding 605,653 shares or 7.2 per cent voted against the proposal.
The approval paves the way for the proposed SCR, under which shareholders other than Ajinomoto will receive RM20 cash for each share held, and those shares will subsequently be cancelled.
The exercise involves a total capital repayment of about RM603.4 million for the 30.17 million shares held by shareholders other than Ajinomoto.
Ajinomoto currently owns 50.38 per cent, or about 30.62 million shares, in Ajinomoto Malaysia.
Upon completion of the SCR, the Japanese parent is expected to become the sole shareholder, with Ajinomoto Malaysia to be delisted from the Main Market of Bursa Malaysia.
The RM20 offer represents a 31.6 per cent premium to Ajinomoto Malaysia's last traded price of RM15.20 on June 19, before the privatisation proposal was announced.
It also represented premiums between 30.68 per cent and 49.93 per cent to the company's five-day and one-year volume-weighted average market prices at the time of the offer.
Ajinomoto first announced the privatisation proposal on June 22, stating its intention to consolidate full ownership of its Malaysian subsidiary.
As part of the exercise, Ajinomoto Malaysia proposed a 571.1 million-share bonus issue, involving the capitalisation of RM571.1 million from retained earnings, to facilitate the SCR.
Ajinomoto said the privatisation would give its Malaysian unit greater flexibility in pursuing its business strategies and improving operational efficiency.
It would also simplify the company's corporate structure and eliminate costs and management resources associated with maintaining a public listing.

The parent also cited the historically low liquidity of Ajinomoto Malaysia shares, which averaged about 38,715 shares traded daily over the five years preceding the proposal, as a factor behind the offer.

Ajinomoto Malaysia's board, excluding interested directors, accepted the proposal in July after considering advice from independent adviser RHB Investment Bank Bhd and subsequently agreed to table the SCR for approval by disinterested shareholders.
Maybank Investment Bank Bhd was appointed principal adviser for the exercise.
The offer drew differing views over valuation during the privatisation process.
An independent analyst valued the shares at RM26.20 each.
However, Ajinomoto said the RM20 offer reflected the company's size, growth prospects, profitability, financial position and low share liquidity.
For the financial year ended March 31, 2026, Ajinomoto Malaysia reported a 43.9 per cent increase in net profit to RM71.45 million, reflecting a recovery from the previous year's weaker performance.

a8d68ee824d69dc9: GENEVA: Civilians are being hardest hit by surging violence in Yemen between Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthis, the UN human rights chief said on Thursday.
The latest fighting marks a sharp escalation in Yemen's civil war, which had largely been frozen since a 2022 truce.

Violence has flared along old front lines in recent weeks, including around Taiz as the Houthis swept south along the Red Sea coast, prompting a humanitarian crisis with over 130,000 people displaced and some fleeing to Africa across the Red Sea.

UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Turk said his office has documented the killing of 32 civilians, including 15 children and 3 women, since August in fighting, including drone and missile strikes.
"Civilians are now bearing the brunt of this latest upsurge in fighting," Turk said in a statement, without giving a breakdown of who was responsible for the casualties.
A total of 125 people were documented by his office as killed or wounded in the latest flareup in the conflict.
Both sides allege that hundreds have been killed in fighting over the past weeks, without providing details.
The statement said the UN human rights office had documented three attacks by Ansar Allah, the formal name for the Houthi movement, on sites for internally displaced people since August.
It was not immediately clear if the UN toll included any deaths or injuries from those incidents.

Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdulsalam said the UN human rights office was no longer impartial, accusing it of ignoring what he described as Saudi bombardment in Yemen that had targeted public facilities.
He cited what he said was the targeting of inmates at a correctional facility in al-Hazm in al-Jawf province, as well as homes and schools in several areas.
He said the UN allegations were false and unsupported by evidence.
More than 70 UN staff are being detained by Houthis in Yemen, some of whom have been held for many years.
Turk called for their release and urged all the warring parties to protect civilians.
Saudi officials have repeatedly said the country's forces do not target civilians in Yemen.
Saudi Arabia's diplomatic mission to the UN in Geneva did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

2860e72746686721: US defense and homeland security agencies bought digital forensics software developed by the same Russian operation that also sold its wares to the FSB, according to US prosecutors. The Department of Justice says Oxygen Forensics CEO Lee Reiber and Russian national Oleg Sergeyevich Davydov have been arrested and charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud over an alleged scheme to hide the company's Russian ownership and where its software was actually being built. Oxygen Forensics, based in Virginia, sold digital forensics tools to the US Department of War and several Department of Homeland Security components, including Homeland Security Investigations, the DHS Office of Inspector General, and the Secret Service's National Computer Forensics Institute (NCFI). Prosecutors allege Oxygen presented itself to Uncle Sam as an independent US company, when it was actually owned and controlled by five Russian nationals through a Cyprus-based holding company. Those same five people also owned a Russian outfit formerly known as Oxygen Software LLC and now called MKO Systems LLC. According to the DoJ, the developers who wrote the software worked in Russia, while MKO sold the software there under different product names to customers reportedly including the FSB, the Russian Investigative Committee, and the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs. In other words, the prosecutors are claiming that while US agencies bought Oxygen's forensic tools, software from the same Russian development operation was being supplied to some very different government customers back home. The alleged concealment kicked up a gear after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 and Washington expanded sanctions. Prosecutors claim Reiber was installed as Oxygen's CEO, president, and chairman, while its Russian owners disappeared from public corporate filings but continued making significant decisions, such as setting Reiber's compensation, overruling him on payments, and retaining signatory authority over company bank accounts. When a reporter came knocking about Oxygen's Russian links in 2023, Reiber allegedly told the owners the resulting coverage "could destroy this entire opportunity" – a reference to a contract the company was chasing with NCFI. Oxygen's "current existence ... hangs in the balance," he is said to have added. NCFI went on to award Oxygen a five-year software contract in September 2024. According to prosecutors, Oxygen had separately told the Department of Defense that no foreign person had the power to control the company or its decisions. As recently as March 2026, Reiber allegedly told DHS personnel that no Russian was involved in developing the software and nobody in Russia had access to its build environment. The DoJ claims the software was in fact written and managed by a Russian team under Davydov's direction. Reiber was arrested in Idaho, while Davydov was nabbed at London's Heathrow Airport before boarding a flight to Istanbul. The US plans to seek his extradition. Authorities have also seized corporate bank accounts, around 57 domains, and other infrastructure. The DOJ is not alleging that Oxygen's software contained malicious code or was used to gain unauthorized access to customers' systems or data. Both men, if convicted, could be swapping forensic software for prison bars for up to 20 years. ®

d1bb0160985a6915: ORLANDO: The US dollar's surge, propelled by strong US economic data, a hawkish Federal Reserve, and surging bond yields, is gathering momentum.
An increasingly interventionist US Treasury will not welcome this – and it’s a reminder that for market actions to work, governments need to be willing to go big.
The dollar fell 10% last year, its worst year since 2017, and was widely expected to continue that trajectory this year.
At the end of January it was languishing at a four-year low. But it has rebounded 6% since then, with momentum now accelerating sharply.
Further appreciation looks likely. As HSBC analysts put it on Wednesday, "the dollar has been ‘freed from debasement’".
The rally pours cold water on the "dollar debasement" narrative sparked last year.

Foreign investors are clearly not turning against the greenback. That might be welcome news in the White House, but the shift also undercuts some of the Trump administration's key economic goals, including reviving American manufacturing and narrowing the enormous trade deficit, which revolve around a more competitive exchange rate.
Moreover, one of the key drivers of the move – spiking bond yields – is the exact opposite of what the treasury is aiming for.
This all calls into question the interventionist methods in the currency and bond markets that treasury secretary Scott Bessent has resorted to this year.
In late July, the treasury acted alongside Japanese authorities to cool the dollar's sizzling strength against the yen.

Three weeks later, Bessent zeroed in on long-term US borrowing costs, announcing that the treasury would increase the size of scheduled buybacks of long-duration debt, a move most observers saw as an effort to lower the yields on these bonds.
Both of these ventures were proudly trumpeted by Bessent, who later boasted, "I have asymmetric information. I am the house now... You can bet against me if you want."
Well, investors are betting against him. The yen is now right back in the "intervention zone" near 160 per dollar. Meanwhile, long-dated treasury yields are at their highest in 22 years.
The harsh truth is that trying to impose your will on the US$30 trillion US treasury market and US$10 trillion-a-day global foreign exchange (FX) market is not so easy.
Central market firepower

Some government interventions over the decades have been successful. Their primary lessons are that words have to be backed by overwhelming force, the scale needs to be enormous, and, quite often, the moves need to be multilateral.
In the 1980s, the world's most powerful central banks sought to weaken the overvalued dollar.
The “Plaza Accord” of 1985 delivered the huge dollar depreciation they wanted, a slide so strong it required the “Louvre Accord” two years later to slow it down.
Similarly, coordinated intervention to support the fledgling euro in late 2000 marked what is still the currency's all-time low.
When trying to manage government borrowing costs via quantitative easing (QE), size, force, and credibility are key.

This QE policy was first used by the Bank of Japan in the early 2000s and then by the Fed in response to the global financial crisis. It worked, but it took trillions of dollars and yen as well as the clear message that more would be forthcoming if necessary.

In a similar vein, European Central Bank president Mario Draghi's unscripted promise at the height of the eurozone debt crisis in July 2012 to do "whatever it takes" to save the euro was successful largely because markets believed he meant it. Huge bouts of QE followed.
By comparison, the US treasury's recent actions are minute specks on the intervention landscape. Of course, they aren't intended to be comparable.
They're designed to tackle pockets of market illiquidity and unwanted volatility, according to Bessent.
However, even if that’s true, their small size means their chances of achieving anything more than a temporary fix are slim.
So after Bessent proclaimed that he could bring multi-trillion-dollar markets to heel with small actions, the treasury is now facing the highest borrowing costs in decades and a resurgent dollar.

"The biggest impediment to buying the dollar was fear of debasement. The biggest impediment to selling the dollar is (attractive) nominal and real rate differentials," Steven Englander at Standard Chartered said on Wednesday.
The dollar 'debasement' narrative had traction earlier this year when the greenback was at a four-year trough and hurtling lower.
However, the extraordinary rebound in the expected path for US interest rates has nixed that.
Debasement fears, such as they are, appear to be centered on US bonds. Perhaps "the house" doesn’t always win.
(The opinions expressed here are those of Jamie McGeever, a columnist for Reuters)

Sementara itu, mengenai perancangan beliau memastikan platform digital lebih selamat untuk rakyat, Fahmi berkata misi utama kementerian ketika ini ialah melaksanakan kolaborasi rentas kementerian dalam mengawal selia ekonomi digital yang berpaksikan e-dagang.

“Saya jaga sektor telco, sektor kurier... kita nampak ada aduan daripada pemilik kedai sebab sekarang ini, banyak barang yang dijual tidak berkualiti, tiada pemantauan malah terlalu murah sehingga peniaga-peniaga kita, ramai bumiputera yang sangat terkesan.

Beliau juga berkata sekiranya tidak bertindak segera, Malaysia akan dilanda lambakan produk terutama elektrik dan elektronik yang tak menepati piawaian Institut Piawaian dan Penyelidikan Perindustrian Malaysia (SIRIM) serta berisiko kepada pembeli.
27463a1648bf74ad: KUALA LUMPUR: The revocation of the appointments of 10 Negri Sembilan executive council members has been gazetted today.
The gazette was issued by order of the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir.

"Whereas pursuant to Article XXXVIII(5) of the Laws of the Constitution of Negeri Sembilan 1959, a member of the State Executive Council other than the Menteri Besar shall hold office for as long as it has my (Tuanku Muhriz) pleasure," the gazette said.

The 10 are Datuk Mohd Faizal Ramli, Datuk Zaifulbahri Idris, Datuk Mustapha Nagoor, Siow Kong Choon, Siti Nur Umaira Hasim, Datuk Mohd Asna Amin, Datuk Mohd Razi Mohd Ali, Suhaimizan Bizar, Mohd Fairuz Mohd Isa and Datuk Razali Abu Samah.

According to the gazette, all 10 took and signed their oaths of office and pledges of allegiance before Tuanku Muhriz on Aug 7 before assuming office as members of the Negeri Sembilan State Executive Council.

"And whereas, in view of your breach of the said pledge of allegiance, I hereby withdraw my pleasure and revoke your appointments as members of the Negri Sembilan state executive council," the gazette said.

The impasse between the Negri Sembilan palace and the administration has been ongoing since April, when the Undang Yang Empat proclaimed the removal of Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negri Sembilan Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir.
Menteri Besar Datuk Ismail Lasim was reported to be among those who signed the proclamation, although he later claimed that he had done so under duress.
It was then reported that Tuanku Muhriz revoked the exco members' appointments over a breach of their oath.
Earlier today, Ismail said the state executive councillors were barred from entering their offices in Wisma Negeri.

94d2c19f9729439b: KUALA LUMPUR: The government has never used the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) as a political tool to restrict anyone’s freedom of expression, particularly on social media, says communications minister Fahmi Fadzil.
Instead, he said, MCMC plays an important role in regulating social media platforms in the country to safeguard public safety in the digital space.

“There are many misunderstandings, for example regarding the removal of content on social media platforms such as Facebook. It is not a minister who decides, not Fahmi Fadzil, not MCMC, but the platform itself.

“MCMC is a tool for (the safety of) the people. They complain about cyberbullying, the dissemination of intimate images, scams and many other things. So, if people want MCMC's services, then MCMC should serve them,” he said as a guest on The Tiger Show podcast hosted by journalist Amin Iskandar.

Elaborating further, Fahmi said any report and complaint received by MCMC would be referred to the platform providers for further action in accordance with their respective community guidelines and the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998 (Act 588).

“For example, if I complain to MCMC, I make the complaint myself, but it does not necessarily mean the content will be removed. The one removing the content is Facebook or TikTok if they review it and agree that the content violates the law.

“That is why, say, MCMC now sends almost half a million requests to remove content, perhaps only 90% of the total is removed, because this is an action by the platform provider, not a decision made by MCMC,” he said.

Fahmi said all platform providers operating in the country had so far cooperated with the government, particularly in dealing with content touching on racial, religious and royal sensitivities, known as 3Rs.
“However, for things such as satire and mockery, the platforms will usually say that the content does not violate the law,” he said.

Meanwhile, on his plans to make digital platforms safer for the public, Fahmi said the ministry’s current priority was cross-ministry collaboration to regulate the digital economy, particularly e-commerce.

“As I oversee the telco and courier sectors, we receive complaints from shop owners because many goods are now being sold without adequate quality, with no monitoring, and at prices that are too low, which has severely affected many of our traders, including Bumiputera traders.
“So, I want to resolve this together with the finance and domestic trade and consumer affairs ministries,” he said.
Fahmi said without prompt action, the country could face a glut of products, particularly electrical and electronic goods that do not meet Sirim standards and could pose risks to consumers.

d27ca21e427831ee: LONDON: Harry Kane is in line to move level with Peter Shilton as England's most-capped player over the next fortnight, but is wondering why the record of 125 appearances for the national side is not higher.

Kane is currently four short of Shilton's haul but a quartet of Nations League fixtures against Spain, Croatia and the Czech Republic (two) could allow him to equal the celebrated goalkeeper's record.
"Growing up, the dream was just to play for England and being most capped was never even in my mind at that stage," said Kane, the Three Lions' all-time top goalscorer.

"The journey has been incredible to this stage, and we have achieved so much as a group and personally achieved so much and been in finals, taking the England team to a level that it hasn’t been for a long, long time.
"So, to be four away from the all-time is just incredible and hopefully I am able to play the four games and then be back in November and be able to break it," he said.
Kane is just one of 10 men to have reached a century of caps for England.

By contrast, Cristiano Ronaldo has represented Portugal a world-leading 233 times, with contemporaries Lionel Messi (Argentina) and Luka Modric (Croatia) also having passed 200 caps for their respective countries.
Kane’s former Tottenham team-mates Christian Eriksen, Jan Vertonghen and Ivan Perisic are among a variety of modern-day players to have featured in over 150 internationals.
"It makes you wonder why (not) as well with England," added Kane. "Is it a cultural thing? Is it a mentality thing? Is it maybe the pressure from the outside?
"Why have some of our great England players not reached that 160, 170, 180 (caps) like some of the other nations?
"From my point of view, it will be an honour but ultimately there is still a long way to go and still hopefully a lot more caps I can achieve," he added.
Despite his prolific record of 85 international goals, a major tournament victory is the one thing missing from Kane's England career.
A home Euros in two years' time could present his final opportunity and he is targeting Saturday's clash against world champions Spain at Wembley as a chance to lay down a marker.
"Look, we're playing the reigning European champions, the reigning world champions, so it doesn't get any tougher in terms of who we're going to face," he added.

"But ultimately if we want to be Nations League champions, European champions in a couple of years, we're going to have to beat teams like Spain and Croatia and the bigger nations. It’s good for us to test ourselves, test the group," he said.
2aac35017d330c11: KUALA LUMPUR: IHH Healthcare Bhd's subsidiary Northern TK Venture Pte Ltd (NTK) has appealed to the Tokyo High Court against a ruling dismissing its ¥200 billion (about RM5.3 billion) damages claim against Japanese pharmaceutical company Daiichi Sankyo Co Ltd.
The appeal follows the Tokyo District Court's Sept 10 dismissal of all claims brought by NTK and its order for the IHH unit to bear the litigation costs.
IHH said NTK concluded that the matter warranted review by a higher court after assessing the judgment and exercised its right of appeal.
"Having assessed the judgment, NTK concluded that it warrants appellate review by a higher court, and has accordingly exercised its right of appeal," IHH said in a statement today.

The dispute is linked to IHH's 2018 acquisition of a controlling stake in India's Fortis Healthcare Ltd, which subsequently became the subject of legal complications involving Daiichi Sankyo and the former Fortis promoters.
IHH, through NTK, bought a 31 per cent stake in Fortis, but later halted its open offer to acquire a further 26 per cent.
This was after Daiichi Sankyo filed contempt proceedings against the Indian hospital group's founders.
The legal dispute dates back to Daiichi Sankyo's separate battle with former Fortis promoters Malvinder Mohan Singh and Shivinder Mohan Singh.

Daiichi Sankyo had acquired Ranbaxy Laboratories from the Singh brothers in 2008 and subsequently alleged that the brothers had withheld information concerning regulatory issues at the Indian drugmaker.
A Singapore arbitration tribunal in 2016 ordered the brothers to pay Daiichi Sankyo about 25.62 billion Indian rupees in damages, plus interest.
The dispute subsequently spilled over into Fortis, which the Singh brothers controlled.
IHH emerged as a "white knight" in 2018, acquiring a controlling stake through NTK and triggering a mandatory open offer.
IHH has maintained that it suffered losses because of delays in obtaining the mandatory tender offer approvals needed for its Fortis acquisition.
It has also stressed that it was not a party to the dispute between Daiichi Sankyo and the judgment debtors.
NTK initially filed its lawsuit against Daiichi Sankyo in the Tokyo District Court in October 2023, seeking more than ¥20 billion in damages.
It later amended its claim in May 2025 to ¥203.3 billion, according to Daiichi Sankyo.
In its latest statement, IHH reiterated that the Fortis acquisition was undertaken through a transparent, publicly disclosed and fully regulated process.
The transaction received the required corporate, shareholder and regulatory approvals, including those under India's Competition Commission and Securities and Exchange Board of India regulations.
Meanwhile, the legal proceedings have not altered IHH's stated plans for Fortis and its wider India operations.

IHH said India remains a key strategic market and that it plans to increase its stake in Fortis to 51 per cent over the next three to five years, further integrate its Fortis and Gleneagles platforms and expand its capacity in India to about 10,000 beds by 2031.

"As one of the largest and longest-standing foreign direct investors in India's hospital sector, IHH has remained steadfast in its commitment to the country despite the challenges arising from this matter. ," it said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd
