2a36ec411fafb778: Malaysia Day celebrations every September carry a distinct resonance in Sabah and Sarawak. In these two states, unity is not merely a political slogan, but a lived reality. Inter-ethnic and inter-religious frictions are remarkably rare; instead, Bumiputera and non-Bumiputera communities coexist seamlessly as a cohesive people.
While various historical and cultural factors contribute to this social harmony, the most powerful catalyst hiding in plain sight is a linguistic one: the Malay language.
In West Malaysia, linguistic and social circles can remain highly segregated among people, but East Malaysia’s unique demographic tapestry demands a universal bridge.

Sabah and Sarawak are home to dozens of indigenous ethnic groups, including the Kadazan-Dusun, Murut, Iban, and Bidayuh. No single indigenous language dominates the landscape. Malay naturally evolved into the ultimate daily lingua franca, spoken by all and sundry, transcending ethnic divides.

This linguistic embrace is particularly evident among East Malaysia's non-Bumiputera communities, primarily the Chinese. While their counterparts in Peninsular Malaysia often rely on Mandarin, Cantonese, or Hokkien for intra-ethnic communication and may hesitate when speaking the national language, non-Bumiputera in East Malaysia demonstrate remarkable fluency and spontaneity in Malay.

This regional divergence is deeply rooted in the phonetic accessibility of East Malaysian Malay. Structurally, the variants spoken in the East are closer to standard written Malay, making them significantly more intuitive for non-native speakers to master.

For instance, while the standard Peninsular dialect modifies the final "a" into a schwa sound (turning saya into say-uh), Sabahan and Sarawakian Malay preserve the clean, phonetic "a" sound (say-ah). By largely speaking the language exactly as it is written, East Malaysians bypass the pressure of navigating complex vowel shifts or exclusionary slang rules.
Furthermore, the language in East Malaysia has evolved organically into a living, breathing community identity rather than a rigid, institutional subject.

Rather than sticking strictly to textbook constraints, communities speak distinct regional dialects heavily infused with localised slang, indigenous loanwords, and Chinese particle markers. Whether it is the ubiquitous Sabahan "bah" or the distinct Sarawakian pronouns "kamek" and "kitak," this blending strips away structural formality and fosters an authentic, shared ownership of the language.

This linguistic integration is further cemented by the high rates of intermarriage that define East Malaysian society. With far more interracial families than the Peninsula, it is incredibly common for Chinese-Bumiputera households to speak Malay natively at home. This blending effectively blurs the strict cultural and linguistic boundaries seen elsewhere in the country.

Ultimately, the Malay language in Sabah and Sarawak does not just connect different communities; it unites them. By transforming the national language into an accessible, organic, and inclusive medium, East Malaysians offer a profound blueprint for what true national unity can look like.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

DAP bagaimanapun menurut Loke menghormati keputusan Yang di-Pertuan Agong. Bagi saya, ini boleh dieksploitasi parti lawan.
Loke menyifatkan langkah partinya sesuatu yang 'bertanggungjawab'. Hanya beliau seorang letak jawatan, kata Loke, bagi memastikan kerajaan kekal stabil.

Oleh itu, kata Loke, CEC buat keputusan mereka kekal dalam Jemaah Menteri, 'walaupun mereka juga sedia pada mana mana waktu, apa apa ketika (untuk melepaskan jawatan)'.
Sudah tentu golongan yang bukan peminat besar DAP tidak puas hati dengan penjelasan Loke.

Manakala Yeoh menegaskan beliau telah menyatakan kepada lembaga pengampunan pandangannya 'secara jujur, berterus-terang dan berlandaskan hati nurani demi kepentingan negara', serta berdasarkan pendapat undang undang 'setelah meneliti pendapat bertulis peguam negara'.
Apa pun kritikan, serangan dan provokasi pesaing serta pembenci DAP tercetus pantas. Lihat sahaja komen di media sosial dan ruang komen pembaca portal berita. Banyak juga berbaur perkauman.

Sebagai parti politik, tidak boleh dinafikan apa yang dilakukan DAP dan Loke mempunyai elemen kepentingan parti dan kelangsungan politik. Ada penganalis dipetik FMT berpendapat keputusan Loke mungkin tidak dapat reda kemarahan akar umbi DAP terhadap pengampunan bersyarat Najib.

Lau Zhe Wei dari Universiti Islam Antarabangsa Malaysia dipetik berkata, peletakan jawatan beramai-ramai (yakni semua anggota Jemaah Menteri daripada DAP) ialah langkah wajar meskipun DAP tidak bertanggungjawab terhadap pengampunan bersyarat Najib.

Bagi saya, DAP telah menyatakan pendiriannya loud and clear. Ada pemerhati politik beritahu saya, "That’s a strategic withdrawal tactic from Loke and DAP to move forward and to placate the Chinese anger."

Saya setuju ia bertujuan menenangkan hati masyarakat Cina yang rata-rata yakin Najib sudah diberi pengadilan secukupnya lalu mesti pay for his crime. Berdasarkan keputusan mahkamah. Majoriti rakyat Malaysia sependapat.

Bak kata Dr Mahathir Mohamad, Najib sudah diadili oleh Mahkamah Tinggi, Mahkamah Rayuan dan Mahkamah Persekutuan, membabitkan sembilan hakim yang mendapati beliau bersalah (dalam kes SRC International).
Seorang lagi pemerhati politik berkata, keputusan Loke 'is a good move. At least good for DAP supporters'. Maksudnya, penyokong yang bukan ahli parti. Rakyat biasa yang sokong DAP.
Yang jelas, Loke memikul tanggungjawab selaku ketua DAP.

Untuk menutup penulisan kali ini, saya petik catatan Facebook kawan lama Kassim Muhamad, seorang aktivis seni: "Lain padang lain belalang, lain pemimpin politik lain cara melihat tanggungjawab dan pertanggungjawaban. Pengundi bolehlah menilai bagaimana dan kenapa pemimpin politik kekadang tidak sama cara dan tindakannya bila berdepan dengan isu tanggungjawab."
Memang betul, saudara.

d7acaafcd717f3c8: I've spent years building robots that replaced human workers, so I'm no stranger to technological fear, but even I did a double take last week.

On Sept 9, Jacob Coxon, who spent the past three years at OpenAI and then Anthropic, quit with a post on X that has since been viewed more than 100 million times: "Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."

And lest you think this was just one disgruntled ex-employee, Evan Hubinger, who leads Anthropic's alignment science team, agreed that "we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans", putting the odds at more than 10% within the next decade.
But others working in the AI arena see this as fear mongering and a possible sales pitch.
Let me lay out, as fairly as I can, what each camp believes.

Start with the worried camp, who call themselves safety researchers and get called doomers, whose case rests on three planks. The first is that AI capability is climbing faster than our ability to contain it, which is why Coxon warns of "superhuman systems that can hack anything" that will "acquire real power and resources".

The second plank is that the machines are already gaming us. In July, OpenAI ran an internal model through hacking exercises in which, investigators estimate, 30% to 40% of the tasks were impossible. Rather than fail, roughly 1,200 AI agents turned a shared file store into a secret message board, exchanged more than 70,000 messages, faked answers and researched how to tamper with their own transcripts.

About 700 of them then broke into Hugging Face, an external AI hosting company. Investigators at Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR) and Redwood Research found that the agents had "realised this activity was out of scope and unethical" but joined anyway.

The podcaster Dwarkesh Patel, whose essay on the affair went viral, argued in a reply to a critic who said this hacking was "small potatoes" that within years we'll have "hundreds of millions of much smarter AIs". He added that if those AIs were as willing to coordinate in secret to fool us, humanity would be in the position of the Mughals once the East India Company got a foothold in India.

The third plank is the warning and request for guardrails by AI industry leaders. In May 2023, Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and Demis Hassabis signed a statement ranking AI extinction risk alongside "pandemics and nuclear war"; that same month Altman urged the United States Senate to consider "licensing and testing requirements" for models "above a threshold of capabilities".
Now the rebuttal of the other camp, which runs from Silicon Valley's accelerationists to sceptics like Gary Marcus, comes in three parts too. The first is that the fear mongering is a business model.

David Sacks, then the White House AI czar, said last October that "Anthropic is running a sophisticated regulatory capture strategy based on fear-mongering", and Stanford's Andrew Ng wrote that proprietary providers "would hate to have to compete with free, opensource software, and have lobbied intensely for regulations to kneecap it".
Amodei calls such claims "inaccurate" and says his proposals would spare smaller labs.

The second part is to read the July incident again, minus the dramatic language. Marcus points out that the agents got into Hugging Face through API keys left in public code repositories, and that OpenAI had given thousands of agents write access to a shared directory. He concluded that "the scandal is the inept in-house security at OpenAI".

In this telling, a badly designed exam with unlocked doors produced cheating, not Skynet. In case you missed the Terminator movies, Skynet is the fictional AI system that triggers a global nuclear war.

The third part is what caution costs. A licence written in Washington binds only American companies, as June showed: the US Commerce Department ordered Anthropic to cut off foreign nationals from Claude Fable 5, and the model went dark worldwide for nearly three weeks while every rival, OpenAI included, carried on.

Stanford's 2026 AI Index puts the best Chinese model a mere 2.7% behind America's best, and DeepSeek's top model charges RM16 per million output tokens to Anthropic's whopping RM204, so a pause, this camp says, is a gift to China.

There's also what a pause would leave undiscovered, because AI is already saving lives, not merely promising to, they argue. Google DeepMind's AlphaFold, an AI that works out the three-dimensional shape of proteins, the starting point for new drugs, mapped 200 million of them and won its creators a Nobel Prize.

Then there's personalised cancer care. Moderna and Merck's melanoma vaccine is built for each patient, whose tumour is sequenced so an algorithm can pick up to 34 of its mutations to target. Those who received it alongside immunotherapy had a 49% lower risk of recurrence or death after five years in an early trial, a finding a 1,137-patient Phase 3 trial backed last month.

On the ward, a University of California San Diego AI that watches vital signs and lab results for the first stirrings of sepsis cut deaths from it by 17%, and AI-assisted screening of more than 100,000 Swedish women caught 29% more breast cancers with 44% less radiologist work.
The sceptics ask: What if pausing or slowing down AI progress delays the development of such essential life-saving technologies?

Both camps agree this is the most powerful technology of our lifetimes, and both read the same 70,000 messages those OpenAI agents exchanged in July. One saw a machine learning to conspire; the other saw a lab that forgot to lock its doors.

Whether AI is a tool to be governed or an agent to be feared, and whether the people asking for the brakes should be the ones holding them, is the question that decides everything else, and it deserves a column of its own. Stay tuned.

653144da3f9afc34: From Terence Netto
Hassan Karim's opinion that the conditional pardon for Najib Razak is a “golden opportunity” for Pakatan Harapan, deserves attention – and, more pointedly, exploitation.

Since last November, PH and its component parties have been reeling from electoral setbacks in Sabah, Johor and Negeri Sembilan. Rubbing salt into the wound was the glee displayed by its erstwhile partner Umno over the PH defeats.

It was particularly galling in Negeri Sembilan, where the PKR-led state government was toppled and DAP’s Loke Siew Fook defeated at the hands of an MCA opponent who was cheered on by none other than Umno chief Ahmad Zahid Hamidi.
The fact that Zahid sits next to Loke in the Cabinet did not give the Umno president pause in his quest of electoral spoils. Apparently, all is fair and foul in Cabinet and on the hustings.
If Zahid lacks esprit de corps, PH need not bother about decorum in seeking to exploit Najib’s conditional pardon for electoral advantage.
Equality under the law

However one looks at the pardon and the house arrest arrangement for Najib, it sits ill with ordinary people, who are apt to think that there is one rule for the super-elite and another for the hoi polloi.
This is despite the fact that many people think Najib was a good prime minister, especially during the first 18 months after he took over from Abdullah Ahmad Badawi in 2009.
Nothing grates more on ordinary people’s sense of being underprivileged than seeing the guarantee of equal treatment before the law honoured more in the breach than in the observance.
Also, Umno’s decision to organise a fundraiser for Najib to pay his RM50 million fine in order to fulfil a condition of his house arrest must rank as a faux pas of disastrous proportions.
It is like asking victims to help pay the fine imposed on a felon caught with his hands in the public till.
Public morality

Because the issue of Najib Razak and his responsibility for the financial scandals arising from the 1MDB imbroglio involves questions of public morality and accountability, it is heartening to hear what Amanah deputy president Mujahid Yusof Rawa has said.
Amanah has not particularly distinguished itself in handling these issues because of the space it has conceded to PAS and its president, Abdul Hadi Awang, who have ruled the rhetorical roost.

At any one time, it is difficult to sort out what the PAS supremo is actually saying because his writings and speeches are clouded in jargon. Listeners give up, if for no other reason than that the subject matter has to do with Islam, a subject about which a non-Muslim, especially, must tread with caution.

So, when Mujahid, in criticising Umno and PAS for celebrating the grant of a conditional pardon to Najib, spoke of the tawdriness of the moral compass of both parties, he employed a clarity that was the reverse of Hadi’s opacity.
“What has happened to the moral compass of our Malay people?” Mujahid said.

“It’s time the Malays made an important decision for the sake of their dignity. Don’t allow Malay dignity to be represented by those who normalise crime, otherwise our future generations will consider corruption as heroics for the Malay people,” the Amanah leader said plaintively.
PH has been on the back foot for some years now, a consequence of Anwar Ibrahim’s strange loss of effectiveness and clarity of vision.
The “golden opportunity” presented by Najib’s conditional pardon and Umno’s fundraising are a shot in the foot by Umno and PAS that PH must exploit to the hilt.
A gift horse is not to be looked at in the mouth.
